name: The Carlyle Group

summary.text: The Carlyle Group is a Washington, D.C.-based global investment firm founded in 1987 by Bill Conway, Dan D'Aniello and David Rubenstein, which went public in 2012. Former U.S. officials have held publicly reported roles at the firm: Frank Carlucci, a former secretary of defense, was managing director from 1989, chairman from 1993 to 2003 and then chairman emeritus; former president George H.W. Bush was senior adviser to Carlyle's Asia advisory board until 2003; and Fortune reported in 2002 that former secretary of state James Baker, former budget director Richard Darman and former British prime minister John Major also worked for the firm. In Korea, Carlyle and J.P. Morgan Corsair bought a controlling stake in KorAm Bank in 2000 for about US$430-450 million and sold it to Citigroup in 2004 in a transaction valuing the bank at about KRW 3.18 trillion (US$2.73 billion).

facts.claim: Carlyle says it was founded in 1987 by its three founders, Bill Conway, Dan D'Aniello and David Rubenstein. Its 2012 registration statement describes Conway as formerly senior vice president and chief financial officer of MCI Communications, D'Aniello as formerly vice president for finance and development at Marriott Corporation for eight years, and Rubenstein as a Washington lawyer who was Deputy Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy from 1977 to 1981.

facts.claim: Frank Carlucci, U.S. secretary of defense for the final 14 months of the Reagan administration and earlier national security adviser and deputy director of the CIA, became managing director of the Carlyle Group in 1989, chairman in 1993 and chairman emeritus in 2003. As chairman from 1993 to 2003 he oversaw Carlyle's global expansion, including the opening of its first Asian office in Hong Kong. He died June 3, 2018.
facts.quote: after his public service he became managing director of the Carlyle Group in 1989, chairman in 1993, and chairman emeritus in 2003 ... as chairman of Carlyle from 1993 until 2003, Carlucci expanded into industries such as global communications ... and opened its first Asian office, in Hong Kong

facts.claim: Former president George H.W. Bush served as a senior adviser to Carlyle's Asia advisory board, advising the firm's Asian investment funds until he left Carlyle in 2003, according to the Center for Public Integrity. Fortune reported in March 2002 that Bush, former secretary of state James Baker, former secretary of defense Frank Carlucci, former White House budget director Richard Darman, former SEC chairman Arthur Levitt and former British prime minister John Major all worked for Carlyle, and that figures like Bush, Baker and Major were a draw for investors.

facts.claim: In 2000 a consortium led by Carlyle with J.P. Morgan Corsair (JPMorgan Partners) bought a controlling stake in KorAm Bank, Carlyle's first equity investment in a Korean financial-services firm. Reports differ on the terms: US$450 million (Korea Economic Daily; FinanceAsia, for a 40.5% stake) or US$430 million for a 36% stake (Korea Herald).
facts.quote: The investment will mark Carlyle's first equity deal for a South Korean financial services firm in two decades since it invested $450 million in then KorAm Bank in 2000 ... Carlyle and J.P. Morgan Corsair bought a 40.5% controlling stake in the bank for just $450 million

facts.claim: In February 2004 Citigroup agreed to acquire KorAm Bank, described by Carlyle as the sixth-largest commercial bank in Korea, from the investor consortium led by Carlyle and J.P. Morgan Corsair II and through a tender offer, at a total price for 100% of the shares of about KRW 3.18 trillion (US$2.73 billion); the consortium held about 36.55% and agreed to sell at the tender price.
facts.quote: Citigroup agreed to buy 36.55% of the shares of KorAm Bank from the consortium

facts.claim: Citigroup's tender offer for KorAm closed with about 60.9% of outstanding shares validly tendered, giving Citigroup with the consortium's shares about 97.5% of KorAm; Citigroup's 2004 annual report states it acquired 99.8% of KorAm's outstanding shares for a total of KRW 3.14 trillion (US$2.7 billion).
facts.quote: Approximately 60.9% of the outstanding shares were validly tendered and not withdrawn before the offer expired ... acquired 99.8% of KorAm's outstanding shares for a total of KRW 3.14 trillion ($2.7 billion)

facts.claim: In October 2001 CNN/Time, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported that the bin Laden family of Saudi Arabia had invested $2 million in an investment fund run by the Carlyle Group, a merchant bank specializing in buyouts of defense companies. Fortune later reported that the family had been investors in at least one Carlyle fund, with the commitment put at just over $2 million; a Carlyle spokesman said the stake was bought out after September 11 for image reasons.
facts.quote: the family has invested $2 million in an investment fund run by the Carlyle Group, a merchant bank specializing in buyouts of defense companies.

facts.claim: By the end of October 2001 Carlyle and the bin Laden family severed their financial ties; Aviation Week reported the decision was mutual and that the family sold back a $2.02 million investment, principally because of its stake in a Carlyle fund that invests in buyouts of military and aerospace companies. Fortune reported that Carlyle had come under public pressure to cut ties after September 11 because it was a U.S. firm particularly active in the aerospace and defense sectors.
facts.quote: The decision was mutual, with the bin Laden family selling back its $2.02-million investment, principally because of its stake in a Carlyle Group fund that invests in buyouts of military and aerospace companies.

openQuestions: KorAm Bank was not state-owned; no handoff record was written for it. The 2000 stake size (36%, 37% or 40.5%) and price (US$430 million or US$450 million) differ across Korea Herald, AltAssets, FinanceAsia and KED Global; the month of the 2000 purchase was not retrieved.

James Baker's exact Carlyle title and dates (senior counselor, 1993-2005) come from a secondary listing and should be confirmed from Carlyle disclosures or dated press reports. George H.W. Bush's start date (April 1998 per a secondary listing) likewise.

An encyclopedia summary said Carlyle put George W. Bush on the board of its subsidiary Caterair in 1990; not recorded here because no primary or major-outlet source was retrieved. The site has an entity 'george-w-bush'.
Wikipedia lists five original partners (adding Stephen Norris and Greg Rosenbaum, who left in 1995 and 1987); Carlyle's own site names three founders.

Widely repeated accounts say Carlyle held its annual investor conference at the Ritz-Carlton in Washington on September 11, 2001, attended by Shafiq bin Laden, Frank Carlucci and James Baker, with George H.W. Bush attending the previous day, and cite a Washington Post profile of David Rubenstein ("Connections And Then Some", March 2003). The Post article exists at https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/2003/03/16/connections-and-then-some/faaece9e-0225-4310-a8f9-8137d2329d52/ but its text was not retrieved in this session, and the only sources returned describing the conference were advocacy sites, so the item was not recorded as a fact.

Secondary accounts say the $2 million committed in 1995 to Carlyle Partners II was an initial contribution that grew, and Dan Briody's 2003 book quotes a bin Laden family representative saying the figure was much larger; Carlyle's statement that the family was in for $2 million of a $1.3 billion fund and the reported October 26, 2001 severance date (attributed to the New York Times) were not confirmed from primary sources.

The Carlyle spokesman quoted as saying the stake was bought out for image reasons (Chris Ullman, per a January 2002 wire report mirrored on GlobalSecurity.org) should be confirmed against the original AP or newspaper report.
